To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) smart bikeshare systems are not inherently unethical, but are susceptible to unethical design and implementation, (2) the ethics of smart bikeshare can be addressed in design through a critical approach that considers the needs and desires of all stakeholders and (3) smart bikeshares are not only about the technology, but also the sociotechnical arrangements and the relationships that emerge from them

(1) the design of smart bikeshare systems should be informed by an ethical framework which acknowledges the role of technology in the creation of social and economic inequalities; (2) the design of such systems should be informed and shaped by the needs and interests of the communities which use them; and (3) the design of systems should be informed in ways which are sensitive to the needs of the most vulnerable members of those communities.
1) The ethical design of smart bikeshare systems requires the recognition of the agency of users in shaping their own experience of the system.

we need a more critical, more reflexive, more ethical approach to smart bike share design.
we need to design for the people, not the people for the design.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of smart bikeshare systems can be a powerful mechanism for the production of ethical and inclusive urban spaces.
the design of smart systems must be sensitive to the ways in which they are used by citizens, and the ways in which their use is shaped by social, economic and political forces.

ethical considerations should be central to the design of smart systems, particularly in the context of urban mobility, and that the design process can be a site for the development of ethical practices and values.
